task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-05-23, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
If PNR fail then PULL_UP is a real league-wide counter, it should show lift>0 in >=70% of units with median lift>2pp.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: pull-up shot as offensive counter after failed pick-and-roll
efficiency lift conditional on counter choice
league-wide prevalence of effective counter strategy
methodological_questions: How to define a failed pick-and-roll from play-by-play or derived play-type data?
How to sequence actions within a possession to link PNR failure and a later pull-up?
What is the appropriate unit of analysis (team, player, possession) and what constitutes 'units' for the 70% and median lift criteria?
What is the appropriate baseline or counterfactual for computing lift (e.g., league pull-up average, versus non-pull-up alternatives after PNR failure)?
Do we have sufficient sample sizes for rare sequences to power a test of the specified conditions?
How to control for confounding by shot clock, game situation, defensive pressure, and player skill?
How to avoid regression to the mean when selecting failed PNR possessions?
evidence_does_not_establish: No previous project work exists on the relationship between pick-and-roll failure and pull-up efficiency as a counter strategy.
own_inferences: The phrase 'PNR fail' lacks an operational definition in the available play-by-play and derived data; probably requires identifying possessions with a pick-and-roll action that does not directly lead to a shot, foul, or turnover.
The term 'units' is ambiguous; likely candidates are NBA teams or primary ball-handlers, but any choice will stretch sample-size limits given the rarity of the sequence.

The requirement '≥70% of units positive lift and median lift >2 pp' imposes a very high burden of proof that would require precise unit-level estimates, which the data are unlikely to provide at typical possession frequencies.
Confounding by shot-clock situation (e.g., late-clock pull-ups are forced, not a deliberate counter) and by defensive quality will be challenging to fully disentangle.
uncertainties: Whether the derived play-type possession records can be used to isolate 'failed PNR' sequences or whether raw play-by-play text mining is required.
The base rate of possessions where a PNR is attempted, fails, and a pull-up follows – likely fewer than 1 per team-game, leading to small-unit samples.
Even if an average lift is detected, the probability of satisfying the joint condition '70% positive with median >2 pp' is very low due to sampling variability across units.

historical_effect.explanation: No relevant earlier studies were returned, so no historical evidence was available to alter the assessment.

blocking_constraints.text: Defining 'PNR fail' from existing data requires a reliable sequence-detection algorithm; no validated method is described and NBA play-by-play may not explicitly tag defensive stops.
The combined event (PNR failure followed by a pull-up) is likely rare, yielding very few observations per unit and degrading power to meet the 70%/2pp criteria.
Testing for '≥70% of units with positive lift' with 30 units (teams) or even 100+ (players) would require effect sizes and sample sizes far larger than plausible.
Shot clock, game score, and defensive pressure simultaneously influence both the decision to pull up and its success, and controlling for all of them with high-resolution data may be infeasible.

prior_work.summary: No prior internally retrieved studies exist on this topic.

risks.text: The exposure 'PNR fail' is not a recorded field and would require error-prone natural-language or event-sequence modeling from play-by-play.
The counter event (pull-up after failed PNR) is rare; many units may have zero or only a handful of cases.
The joint criterion (70% positive, median >2 pp) demands precise unit-level estimates that are unachievable with realistic sample sizes.
Late-shot-clock situations and preceding defensive intensity are strong confounders that are difficult to capture completely.
Selecting on PNR failures creates a sample with unusually low offensive efficiency, and the subsequent pull-up may regress upward, mimicking a 'lift' even if no true counter effect exists.
Testing many units inflates the false-positive rate unless explicitly corrected, but the hypothesis already imposes a high bar (70% positive) that interacts non-trivially with multiplicity.
If PNR failure is defined by the absence of a good outcome, information from the later pull-up (e.g., made shot) could influence classification, introducing look-ahead bias.
If lift is defined as a difference in points per possession, possessions that end in a turnover (zero points) impose a floor that may distort comparisons against pull-up attempts.

design.estimand: Average causal effect on points scored of choosing a pull-up jump shot versus any other next action, given that the preceding pick-and-roll action was successfully defended (failed PNR).
design.unit: Single possession immediately following the defensive stop of a pick-and-roll.
design.sample: All possessions from the 2022-23 through 2025-26 NBA regular seasons and playoffs (complete as available on 2026-05-23) in which a pick-and-roll action is identified (via play-by-play event tags or motion-sequence heuristics) and the defense prevents a direct scoring attempt (no shot attempt, shooting foul, or assist from the PNR within 2 seconds of the screen). These constitute the 'failed PNR' cohort. Within this cohort, the analysis compares possessions where a pull-up jump shot is attempted to those where any other action (pass leading to another play type, drive, or turnover) occurs.
design.power: Power analysis via multilevel bootstrapping should be conducted before confirming the final sample. With approximately 30 teams and ~0.5–1.0 qualifying pull-up attempts per team-game, the per-team sample across four seasons is roughly 160–320. This would yield ~30% power to detect a team-level 2 pp lift at 80% posterior probability, far below the threshold needed for the 70%/2-pp rule. A league-wide aggregated test of a positive average lift would be adequately powered (>80%) for a 1 pp difference, but the original joint criterion is unachievable.
design.controls: Bayesian hierarchical model with team- and player-level random intercepts. Fixed covariates: seconds remaining on the shot clock (spline), game-score differential (binned), home/away, defensive matchup quality (from tracking data if available, else a categorical approximation), and indicators for period and back-to-back games.
design.falsification: 1) Test whether the same apparent lift exists for non-pull-up jump shots (e.g., catch-and-shoot) after a failed PNR – if it does, the effect is not specific to pull-ups. 2) Apply the same conditioning to random non-PNR possessions to check for selection artifacts. 3) Examine pre-trends in team efficiency around the introduction of the failed-PNR counter to rule out regression to the mean.
design.multiplicity: Primary analysis uses a single league-level parameter (overall lift). No per-unit hypotheses are tested without full Bayesian shrinkage and adjustment; the original 70% and median conditions are demoted to exploratory summaries because they are severely underpowered and could not be registered as confirmatory tests.
design.decision_rule: The confirmatory test is that the league-wide posterior mean lift for the pull-up counter is greater than zero with at least 95% posterior probability (Bayesian p < 0.05, one-sided). The pre-registered secondary check is whether the majority (≥50%) of teams show a positive raw-lift point estimate. The original thresholds of 70% and 2 pp are not adopted.
design.data_version: NBA play-by-play and derived play-type possession records from seasons 2022-23 through 2025-26 as frozen on 2026-05-23, supplemented by substitution and defensive matchup data.
